analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime to leave a gun unsecured where a child can get it and someone gets hurt.
analysis.headline: The Safe Guns, Safe Kids Act was introduced in February 2023 with 5 Democratic cosponsors, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime, punishable by up to 5 years in prison, to knowingly store a gun in a home in a way that is not secure when a child is likely to get access to it without permission — but only if a child actually gets the gun and uses it in a crime or injures or kills someone. Gun owners stay within the law by keeping the gun in a lockbox, using a safety device, keeping it somewhere a reasonable person would consider secure, or carrying it on or near their person. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and families in homes with firearms are the intended beneficiaries. The bill targets a specific, well-documented tragedy: a child finding an unsecured gun and using it — on themselves, on someone else, or in a crime. By attaching a criminal penalty that applies only after harm occurs, it gives adults in gun-owning households a federal-law reason to use the locks and lockboxes many already own. Millions of American children live in homes with loaded, unlocked firearms, and unintentional shootings by children are a recurring cause of death and injury.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal penalty of up to 5 years in prison for knowingly storing a gun unsafely in a residence where a minor is likely to access it without permission, when that minor then gets the gun and uses it in a crime or injures or kills someone.

Defines safe storage in practical terms the ordinary owner can meet: locking the gun with a secure storage device or safety device, keeping it somewhere a reasonable person would believe secure, or carrying it on or near their person so they can use it readily.

Applies only when harm actually happens, so a gun owner who stores a gun loosely but no child ever touches it faces no charge — a design meant to focus punishment on outcomes rather than police homes.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on gun owners whose unsecured firearm ends up in a child's hands and causes harm: they would face fines and up to 5 years imprisonment. Gun owners who already lock up their firearms bear essentially no cost. The firearms industry could face modest pressure from the storage-device requirement, though the bill does not mandate any purchase — an owner can satisfy it by any secure arrangement. The main political cost is borne by members who would have to vote on a gun measure in districts where gun policy is contested.
analysis.who_pays_short: Owners of unsecured guns, after harm occurs

drawbacks.text: The penalty only triggers after a child is already hurt or dead, so it does nothing to prevent the first tragedy in any household — it punishes after the fact rather than requiring secure storage up front.

Criminal liability for an accident in one's own home raises concerns for gun owners about prosecutorial discretion and second-amendment objections; no bipartisan support materialized — all 5 cosponsors were Democrats.

The trigger requires that the owner 'knows or reasonably should know' a minor is likely to access the gun, which in a household where a child lives may be nearly always true, creating a serious legal risk for owners who make a genuine storage mistake.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but the design is deliberately narrow: it cannot prevent the first tragedy because it attaches liability only once a child has used the gun and someone is hurt or a crime has occurred. Its value is deterrence — the threat of federal prison pushing owners to use locks they already own — rather than prevention by mandate. The cost is borne narrowly by owners whose negligence ends in harm, though honest critics point out the same negligence that leads to a prosecution also meant a child had access to a loaded gun for months or years without any intervention. A stronger bill would have required safe storage up front; this one is a compromise designed to be constitutionally and politically palatable, and even it could not get a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the two-year Congress, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI), joined by Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-MI), introduced the bill on February 21, 2023.
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day and never received any further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor consideration — in the entire 118th Congress.
Five Democratic representatives cosponsored the bill and no Republicans did.
The bill's gun-storage provisions amend the federal firearms statute to impose criminal penalties on unsafe home storage when a minor obtains the gun and causes harm.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything affirmative from the bill dying, but the status quo was preserved: owners of unsecured firearms face no federal storage penalty, and members who preferred not to vote on gun-storage rules never had to. Anyone opposed to federal firearms regulation kept the ground unchanged at no cost.

for.name: Rep. Elissa Slotkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Safe Guns, Safe Kids Act and gathered 5 cosponsors; a moderate Democrat from a swing district where gun ownership is common.

for.name: Rep. Hillary Scholten
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only named co-sponsor at introduction.

for.name: 5 Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support; all were Democrats, and no Republican signed on at any point.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 21, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the remainder of the Congress, which kept the bill off the floor.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the floor calendar for the 118th Congress and never brought the bill up; with no committee action, it could not reach a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship and cosponsorship came from Democrats — the sponsor plus 5 Democratic cosponsors, zero Republicans — and the bill died in a committee controlled by the House Republican majority without ever reaching a vote.

industries.note: The bill does not directly regulate manufacturers, but a federal storage-crime standard pressures the industry's customer base and, historically, industry groups have opposed mandatory-storage legislation as a step toward broader gun regulation. Some makers also sell locks and safes, so the storage norm cuts both ways. Its material financial impact is small because liability attaches to individual owners only after harm occurs.

Owners who lock up their guns would face no new burden; owners who store firearms unsecured would face up to 5 years in prison if a child gets the gun and someone is hurt or a crime occurs. Most gun-owning households include children or are visited by them, so the exposure is broad even if prosecutions would be rare.
